title: Circle Wins Final OCC Approval for First National Digital Currency Bank, a National Trust Bank That Can Hold Assets but Cannot Take Deposits or Make Loans
summary: The US Office of the Comptroller of the Currency has given Circle final approval to set up First National Digital Currency Bank, N.A., a national trust bank to be known as Circle National Trust that will start with fiduciary digital asset custody for Circle and its affiliates; it cannot take cash deposits or make loans, and USDC issuance will sit in a New York trust company.
description:
Circle Internet Group, the company behind the USDC stablecoin, has won final approval from the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, the US regulator of national banks, to set up a national trust bank. The details in this article come from The Block's report of the approval, published on July 10, 2026 and updated on October 19, 2026. The report is secondary reporting of the company's announcement, and the OCC's approval letter was not reviewed. Some headlines have called the new entity a crypto-focused national bank; the report's description is narrower, and this article follows it.

What was approved

The OCC granted Circle final approval to establish First National Digital Currency Bank, N.A., which will operate as Circle National Trust. The company announced the approval on Friday, July 10, 2026. A national trust bank is a bank chartered by the OCC whose business is limited mainly to fiduciary activities, such as holding assets on behalf of clients. It sits under direct federal supervision by the OCC, in contrast with a company that relies on state-level licences. Circle's chief executive, Jeremy Allaire, said the federal oversight sets a new standard for transparency, governance and scale.

What the bank can and cannot do

According to the report, at launch the bank will provide fiduciary digital asset custody for Circle and its affiliates. Depending on demand, it may later offer custody to a limited number of institutional clients, mainly banks and other financial institutions. It cannot accept cash deposits or make loans, although it can hold customer assets. A trust bank therefore does not compete with a high-street bank for savings accounts or mortgages; its function is safekeeping.

The report draws a distinction that is easy to overlook. Managing the USDC reserve, the pool of assets that backs the stablecoin, was a key goal of Circle's original application, which was filed on June 30, 2025. Under the terms of the conditional approval, however, that is now a future capability and not part of the launch. USDC issuance itself will move to a New York limited-purpose trust company, and not to the national trust bank. A reader who assumes the new bank will immediately hold the reserves behind USDC would therefore be mistaken on the basis of this report.

The approval timeline

June 30, 2025: Circle applied to the OCC.

December 2025: Circle received conditional approval, alongside Ripple, BitGo, Fidelity Digital Assets and Paxos.

July 10, 2026: final approval was announced, roughly 12 months after the application was filed, a span calculated here from the two dates.

Other firms in the queue

The report places the Circle decision in a wider wave of crypto-related charter applications. BitGo received full OCC approval in December 2025. Crypto.com and Coinbase have won conditional approvals. Bridge, which is owned by Stripe, received conditional approval in February 2026. Sony Bank's trust subsidiary, Connectia Trust, which plans to issue a dollar-backed stablecoin, has cleared the conditional stage. Anchorage Digital Bank was the only crypto firm holding a national trust charter before these approvals; it received its charter in 2021. The report lists many other applicants, including Ripple, Paxos, Coinbase, Crypto.com, World Liberty Financial, Laser Digital, Payoneer, Morgan Stanley, Zerohash, Charles Schwab, EDX, Payward and Catena Labs. Not all of these have received approvals, and the report does not give decisions for each one.

Criticism

Senator Elizabeth Warren has criticised the OCC for granting national trust charters to companies that, in her view, do not qualify under the National Bank Act. The report summarises her position and does not give the OCC's response. The disagreement concerns whether firms whose main business is digital assets fit the legal definition of a national trust bank, a question that could be tested in later challenges.

Company background

The report notes that Circle was the first company to receive a BitLicense from the New York Department of Financial Services, in 2015, and that it also holds licences in the United Kingdom, Singapore and Bermuda. It gives Circle's shares (ticker CRCL) as closing at roughly $63 on the Thursday before the announcement. The report does not say how the shares moved afterward, so this article does not repeat claims about the size of any share-price rise.

What changes for users

For holders of USDC, the report describes no change at launch: issuance moves to a New York trust company, and the new federally chartered bank begins with custody for Circle and its affiliates. The practical effect of the charter, therefore, is mostly about the supervision of Circle's own custody operations and the option of serving a small number of institutional clients later. Whether that becomes a larger business depends on demand and on future OCC decisions about permitted activities.

What to watch

Three points follow from the report. First, whether and when the OCC allows the bank to take on reserve management, since that was the original aim. Second, whether the bank begins serving outside institutions and how many. Third, whether the legal challenge Warren's criticism points to materialises, which would affect not only Circle but the other applicants in the queue.

Limits

This article relies on one secondary report and does not reproduce the OCC's approval. It does not assess Circle's financial position. It is general information, not investment advice.

key_points: Circle announced on July 10, 2026 that the OCC had granted final approval to establish First National Digital Currency Bank, N.A., which will operate as Circle National Trust under direct federal oversight.

At launch the bank will provide fiduciary digital asset custody for Circle and its affiliates, and later it may offer custody to a limited number of institutional clients, mainly banks and other financial institutions.

It cannot accept cash deposits or make loans; managing the USDC reserve was a goal of the original June 30, 2025 application but is a future capability, and USDC issuance will move to a New York limited-purpose trust company.

Conditional approval came in December 2025 alongside Ripple, BitGo, Fidelity Digital Assets and Paxos, and BitGo has since received full approval while Coinbase, Crypto.com and Stripe-owned Bridge hold conditional approvals.
Senator Elizabeth Warren has criticised the OCC for granting national trust charters to companies she says do not qualify under the National Bank Act.
why_it_matters: A stablecoin issuer is moving part of its operations inside the federal banking perimeter, but the charter is narrower than the headline 'crypto bank' suggests. It is a custody-focused trust bank, not a deposit-taking lender, and what it can do at launch is limited.

title: Fed Chair Warsh Names 15 Outside Co-Leaders for Five Task Forces on Communications, the Balance Sheet, Data, Productivity and Jobs, and Inflation, With No Deadlines Set
summary: On July 9, 2026 the Federal Reserve Board announced five task forces to advance the conduct of monetary policy, each co-led by three outside advisers, covering communications, balance sheet policy, data, productivity and jobs, and inflation frameworks; the release gives no timelines or reporting dates.
description:
On July 9, 2026, the Federal Reserve Board announced the leadership and objectives of five task forces it has created to advance the conduct of monetary policy. The announcement came in a press release issued at 3:00 p.m. Eastern time. This article reports what that release says, and it is careful to separate what is stated from what is not. The release names the groups, their objectives and their co-leaders. It does not set deadlines, promise policy changes or describe how the Federal Open Market Committee, known as the FOMC, will use the results.

What the Fed said it is doing

Chairman Kevin Warsh said the goal is "to ensure the Fed is best positioned to achieve our objectives in this consequential time." Each task force is co-led by external advisers, a group the release describes as including economists, business leaders and former central bank practitioners. Federal Reserve staff support the task forces, which are described as operating independently. Their mandate is to follow the evidence, provide candid feedback and produce rigorous findings for the FOMC, the committee that sets the Fed's interest rate target.

Each of the five groups has three co-leaders, which gives 15 outside advisers in total, calculated here. The release lists the co-leaders and their affiliations. It does not separately identify other members or chairs.

The five task forces

The first is Communications. Its objective is to review how the Fed conveys its policy deliberations and decisions under uncertainty. Its co-leaders are Peter R. Fisher, a professor of practice at the Foster School of Business at the University of Washington; Arminio Fraga, founder and chairman of Gávea Investimentos and a former president of the Central Bank of Brazil; and Mervyn King, a former governor of the Bank of England.

The second is Balance Sheet Policy. It is to examine the costs, benefits and institutional implications of the Fed's current balance sheet regime. Its co-leaders are Karen Dynan, a professor of economics at Harvard University; Raghuram Rajan, a professor of finance at the University of Chicago Booth School of Business and a former governor of the Reserve Bank of India; and Jeremy Stein, a professor of economics at Harvard and a former member of the Federal Reserve Board.

The third is Data. Its objective is to improve the quality and timeliness of the real economic signals that inform policy judgments. Its co-leaders are Raj Chetty, a professor of economics at Harvard; Doug McMillon, the former president and chief executive of Walmart; and Kevin Murphy, a professor of economics at the University of Chicago.

The fourth is Productivity and Jobs. It is to assess the economic impact of new general-purpose technologies, including artificial intelligence, to inform policy judgments. Its co-leaders are Marc Andreessen, a cofounder and general partner at Andreessen Horowitz; Charles I. Jones, a professor of economics at Stanford University who the release says is currently on leave at Anthropic; and Asha Sharma, an executive vice president at Microsoft and the chief executive of its Xbox business.

The fifth is Inflation Frameworks. It is to revisit how the Fed understands and responds to the drivers of inflation. Its co-leaders are Greg Mankiw, a professor of economics at Harvard and a former chairman of the Council of Economic Advisers; Thomas Sargent, a professor of economics at New York University and a Nobel laureate; and William White, a senior fellow at the C.D. Howe Institute and a former economic adviser at the Bank for International Settlements.

Who the co-leaders are

The release describes the co-leaders as a mix of academics, business leaders and former central bankers, and the affiliations it gives bear that out. Among the 15, the release identifies economists at Harvard, the University of Chicago, Stanford and New York University, former central bank leaders from Brazil, the United Kingdom and India, a former Federal Reserve governor, and executives from the technology and retail sectors. Because the release lists only the co-leaders, this article does not describe the wider membership of any group.

What is not in the release

Several things that readers may expect are absent. The release gives no timelines, reporting dates or interim deliverables. It says only that more information will be posted periodically on the Fed's website. It does not say whether the groups' findings will be published, whether the FOMC will be required to respond to them, or whether any change to the Fed's framework, communications or balance sheet is planned. It does not state a budget or the number of staff assigned. It does not say how the co-leaders were chosen or whether they receive compensation. It does not mention the current interest rate target or any upcoming testimony to Congress.

How to read the announcement

The announcement is best read as an organizational step rather than a decision on policy. It establishes subjects for review and names the people who will lead the work. The objectives are phrased as reviews, assessments and examinations, and the release does not say what conclusions are expected. Any effect on interest rates, on the size of the Fed's balance sheet or on how officials speak to markets would depend on later decisions that the release does not describe.

The range of topics is notable. Two of the groups, Communications and Inflation Frameworks, concern how the Fed explains and understands its own work. One, Balance Sheet Policy, concerns an instrument the Fed uses in addition to interest rates. One, Data, concerns the information on which judgments rest. The last, Productivity and Jobs, concerns the effect of artificial intelligence and other new technologies on the economy. The release links this last topic to policy judgments but does not say what the Fed currently believes about those effects.

What to watch

The release says updates will be posted periodically. Readers can watch the Fed's website for any publication of findings, any schedule that is announced, and any statement from the FOMC about how the work will be used. Until then, the announcement tells readers who will lead the reviews and what each is asked to examine, and little more. This article is a summary of a public announcement and is not financial advice.

key_points: The Federal Reserve Board announced on July 9, 2026 the leadership and objectives of five task forces to advance the conduct of monetary policy, with Chairman Kevin Warsh saying the aim is to ensure the Fed is best positioned to achieve its objectives.

The five task forces cover communications, balance sheet policy, data, productivity and jobs, and inflation frameworks, and each is co-led by three outside advisers, 15 in total, drawn from academia, business and former central banking.
Fed staff support the task forces, which operate independently and are meant to follow the evidence, give candid feedback and produce findings for the Federal Open Market Committee.
The release gives no timelines, reporting dates or interim deliverables, and says more information will be posted periodically on the Fed's website.
The Productivity and Jobs task force is charged with assessing the economic impact of new general-purpose technologies, including artificial intelligence.
why_it_matters: The Fed's decisions on interest rates and its balance sheet affect borrowing costs for households, businesses and governments. A formal review of how it communicates, uses data and thinks about inflation is a signal about the questions its chair wants examined, although the release itself sets no deadlines and promises no policy changes.

title: India's Finance Ministry Launches a Common Portal for Unclaimed Financial Assets as Part of 'Your Money, Your Right', but It Is a Search Gateway and Not a Claims Engine
summary: The Department of Financial Services has launched a common portal for unclaimed financial assets at unclaimedassetsportal.in, developed with PSB Alliance, that links users to search facilities run by banks, insurers, mutual funds and other institutions, while the article reporting it says it does not explain how claims are filed and notes that only Rs 5,729 crore of Rs 1.44 lakh crore transferred to RBI's DEAF fund has been refunded.
description:
India's Department of Financial Services, part of the finance ministry, has launched a common portal for unclaimed financial assets. The details in this article come from a Moneylife report dated June 1, 2026, which says the launch took place at a review meeting of public sector banks in the previous week. Moneylife is an Indian personal-finance outlet, and parts of its report are its own commentary. The government's own notification was not reviewed. In this article, 1 lakh is 100,000, 1 crore is 10 million, and 1 lakh crore is 1 trillion rupees.

What was launched

The portal is at www.unclaimedassetsportal.in. It was developed with the PSB Alliance, a group of public sector banks, and was launched by the secretary of the Department of Financial Services, M Nagaraju. It covers unclaimed bank deposits, insurance claims, shares, dividends and mutual fund investments. According to the report, it acts as a single gateway that links users to search facilities run by banks, insurers, mutual funds and other institutions, so that people do not have to visit each institution's website separately. It forms part of the Department's 'Your Money, Your Right' campaign, which involves financial regulators and banks. Nagaraju is quoted as saying the portal would significantly improve citizen convenience by offering several search facilities on one platform.

The systems that already existed

Before this launch, people had to use several separate systems. The report lists the Reserve Bank of India's UDGAM portal for bank deposits, the Securities and Exchange Board of India's MITRA platform for mutual funds and securities, the insurance regulator IRDAI's Bima Bharosa for insurance, the Ministry of Corporate Affairs' Investor Education and Protection Fund for shares and dividends, and the Employees' Provident Fund Organisation's systems for provident fund money. The report does not say whether the new portal connects to each of those systems directly or simply points users to institutions' own search tools, so this article does not claim a direct link to any particular one. The report mentions the investor protection fund authority only as a coordinator of the campaign.

How much is at stake

The report offers several figures, with their sources. Over Rs 2 lakh crore was in inactive bank accounts approaching unclaimed status, according to Moneylife's reporting in August 2024. Banks transferred Rs 1.44 lakh crore to the Reserve Bank's Depositor Education and Awareness Fund over five years, but only Rs 5,729 crore was refunded to claimants. Dividing the second figure by the first, an exercise done here and not in the report, indicates that about 4% of the transferred money has been refunded. A petition in the Supreme Court by Aakash Goel cites more than Rs 3.5 lakh crore in unclaimed assets; the Court has issued notice, and the outcome is pending. These figures are measured at different dates and on different bases, so they should not be added together or treated as a single total.

The earlier campaign

The earlier campaign, called Aapki Poonji Aapka Adhikar, ran from October to December and returned Rs 1,887 crore to claimants and nominees, according to the report. Nagaraju acknowledged that this figure may seem modest and described it as the initial impact of awareness-building. Set beside the Rs 5,729 crore refunded from the Depositor Education and Awareness Fund, the campaign figure is a useful reference for what outreach can achieve, though the report does not say whether the two sums overlap.

What the portal does not do

The report is explicit that the portal is a search gateway. It does not explain how claims are filed or processed. Moneylife adds a critical note: banks often fail to publish lists of unclaimed accounts, demand excessive documentation and delay legitimate claims, and these problems hit senior citizens and legal heirs hardest. These are the publication's assessments and not findings of the government. The report says the Supreme Court's response and the government's regulatory response remain open questions.

What a person can do now

Anyone looking for a relative's savings or an old policy can search through the portal, and can also use the regulators' own tools that the report lists. A claimant will generally need to establish identity and, for an heir, a legal connection to the account holder, and the process differs by institution. The report does not set out the steps, so claimants should follow the instructions of the institution that holds the money.

What to watch

Three points will show whether the portal makes a difference: whether institutions keep their data current, whether claim processing times fall, and whether the amounts returned each year rise above the levels the report cites. The report gives no targets for any of these.

Why the numbers are hard to compare

The report mixes three kinds of figures: balances in accounts approaching dormancy, money already transferred to a regulator-run fund, and amounts returned to claimants. Each answers a different question. The first says how much might one day become unclaimed, the second how much has already left banks' books, and the third how much has actually reached owners. Only the third measures success for the people the portal is meant to serve.

Limits

This article relies on one publication's report and does not reproduce the government's notification. It is general information, not legal or financial advice.
image_alt: Indian rupee notes and bank documents representing unclaimed deposits (illustrative)
key_points: The Department of Financial Services in India's finance ministry launched a common portal for unclaimed financial assets at www.unclaimedassetsportal.in, developed with the PSB Alliance and launched by DFS secretary M Nagaraju at a review meeting of public sector banks in the week before June 1, 2026.

It covers unclaimed bank deposits, insurance claims, shares, dividends and mutual fund investments, acting as one gateway to search facilities run by banks, insurers, mutual funds and other institutions.
It is part of the DFS-led 'Your Money, Your Right' campaign, and the earlier 'Aapki Poonji Aapka Adhikar' campaign returned Rs 1,887 crore to claimants and nominees between October and December.

Banks transferred Rs 1.44 lakh crore to the RBI's Depositor Education and Awareness Fund over five years, of which only Rs 5,729 crore was refunded to claimants, and a Supreme Court petition cites more than Rs 3.5 lakh crore in unclaimed assets.
The portal is a search gateway; the report says it does not explain how claims are filed or processed, and notes complaints that banks delay legitimate claims and demand excessive documentation.
why_it_matters: Money left in dormant accounts, old policies and uncollected dividends is often hard to trace, especially for heirs. One search point should help people find what they are owed, but the real test is whether claims are then paid quickly, and the launch does not show that yet.

title: The FCA's Mills Review Sets Out Seven Recommendations for an AI-Enabled 2030, After Finding One in Five UK Adults Open to AI Acting on Their Behalf
summary: Published on July 6, 2026, the FCA's Mills Review, led by executive director Sheldon Mills, concludes that financial services are moving toward AI-enabled, continuous and delegated models, proposes no new rules, and makes seven recommendations including adapting the regulatory perimeter and building an AI-enabled supervisory model.
description:
The UK's Financial Conduct Authority has published a review that tries to describe what retail financial services will look like by 2030 once artificial intelligence is built into almost every part of them. The Mills Review, titled "AI and the future of retail financial services", was led by FCA executive director Sheldon Mills and commissioned by the regulator's Board. The FCA published it on July 6, 2026, although the page metadata gives July 3, so readers should check the date on the FCA site. The regulator describes it as the first work of its kind initiated by a regulator anywhere in the world. This article summarises the FCA's press release and a legal analysis from the law firm CMS published on July 10, and it does not replace the report itself.

How the review was done

The FCA launched the review in January 2026 with an engagement paper that closed for responses on February 24. According to CMS, it drew on more than 140 written submissions and on discussions with firms, trade bodies, consumer groups, technology providers and international stakeholders. In April 2026, Yonder Consulting surveyed more than 5,000 UK retail financial services consumers, with quotas set to make the sample representative. The review builds on earlier FCA work on AI, including its 2023 discussion paper, the AI Sprint, the AI Lab, the AI Live Testing programme, whose second cohort has been announced, and the Supercharged Sandbox, which is supported by NVIDIA.

The central finding

The review's main conclusion, as described by CMS, is that financial services are shifting from human-led, episodic activity toward services that are AI-enabled, continuous and delegated. It uses a five-level spectrum of autonomy, running from humans operating AI tools at one end to humans acting only as observers at the other. The review says few services will become fully autonomous, but that most leading firms are expected to embed AI across almost every function by 2030. It also concludes that the existing regulatory framework is broadly sound, though it may come under strain as AI becomes more agentic, meaning able to take actions towards goals with limited human involvement.

Four shifts

The first shift is the transformation of firms. Staff move from being operators of AI to approvers and observers. The review says that being "in the loop" is not enough, and firms must define what oversight involves, what reviewers see and how challenge is recorded. AI governance and model risk management become more important, especially where firms rely on third-party providers.

The second is the evolution of consumer journeys. The FCA's research found that about one in five consumers, around 11 million UK adults, would be likely to use AI that can act autonomously within pre-set goals. CMS reports that demand is strongest for debt advice, pensions and investments, and that about a quarter already trust general-purpose tools for financial guidance. The review sees AI as a way to close gaps: about 9% of people receive regulated advice, about 30% hold life or income protection, and about £300 billion sits in low-interest accounts. It also identifies risks, including bias through hyper-personalisation, opaque pricing and personalised deceptive design. Consumers surveyed raised concerns about data misuse (68%), lack of protection if things go wrong (67%) and power concentrating in large firms (65%).

The third is a reshaping of competition and market power. The review points to control of AI-mediated interfaces, such as agents that search, compare and buy products, to barriers to entry that may fall for digital-native firms while scale favours incumbents, and to concentration in the AI supply chain, which raises concerns about cost, lock-in and resilience.

The fourth is the amplification of fraud and cyber risk. AI will make fraud faster, cheaper, more scalable and more persuasive, with cloned voices, synthetic identities and deepfakes. AI can also strengthen detection, and firms will have to show that their controls improve detection and disruption while keeping meaningful human oversight.

The seven recommendations

The recommendations are addressed to the FCA Board and Executive. They are to secure and adapt the regulatory perimeter; strengthen system-wide coordination and oversight; monitor the transition to autonomous models and adapt regulatory frameworks; scale up the FCA's AI Lab; enable the foundations for agentic finance; build and adopt an AI-enabled agentic supervisory model; and develop a trusted public-interest AI-enabled financial capability service.

CMS adds some detail. On the perimeter, it says that in the short term the FCA should review the scale and impact of general-purpose large language models that sit outside the perimeter but influence consumer financial decisions, and in the long term should seek powers beyond the critical third party regime. On monitoring autonomy, the review is said to flag an open question about the Senior Managers "reasonable steps" obligation without answering it. On foundations, the review suggests a trusted framework for AI agent identity, authority, accountability and execution, ideally through standards developed via Open Finance. On the public-interest service, it envisages a free, inclusively designed AI service giving consumers reliable financial information and guidance.

What it means for firms

CMS notes that the review proposes no specific rule changes, but it is likely to shape supervisory priorities, perimeter policy and future guidance. Firms are advised to map their current and planned AI use against the autonomy spectrum, review governance and senior-manager responsibilities, strengthen auditability, explainability and complaints handling, test AI-driven customer journeys against Consumer Duty outcomes, review operational resilience and third-party dependencies, and strengthen AI-enabled fraud controls while retaining human oversight. The Consumer Duty, which requires firms to deliver good outcomes for retail customers, remains the main lens. FCA Chair Ashley Alder said the regulator's principles-based, outcomes-focused approach, relying on the Consumer Duty and the Senior Managers Regime, has been critical to keeping pace with change.

The FCA said it will publish an AI good and poor practice report later in 2026, based on direct engagement with firms. Insurers and banks using AI in pricing, underwriting, credit decisions and customer service will be watching that report for more specific expectations.

This article is a summary of public documents and commentary and is general information, not legal advice. Firms should read the review and take advice on its application to their business.
source_name: Financial Conduct Authority (press release, July 6, 2026) and CMS legal update (July 10, 2026)
image_alt: Artificial intelligence and data concept representing AI in financial services (illustrative)
key_points: The Mills Review, led by FCA executive director Sheldon Mills, was commissioned by the FCA Board in January 2026 and drew on more than 140 written submissions; the FCA calls it the first work of its kind initiated by a regulator globally.
A Yonder survey of more than 5,000 UK consumers in April 2026 found that about 20%, or around 11 million adults, would likely use AI that can act autonomously within pre-set goals.
The review identifies four shifts: transformation of firms, new consumer journeys, reshaped competition and market power, and amplified fraud and cyber risk.

Its seven recommendations include securing and adapting the regulatory perimeter, strengthening system-wide coordination, scaling up the FCA's AI Lab and developing an AI-enabled agentic supervisory model.
The review proposes no specific rule changes; the FCA says it will publish an AI good and poor practice report later in 2026.
why_it_matters: AI already influences how insurers price risk, how banks assess credit and how customers get help, and the review signals how the UK regulator expects firms to govern it as systems start to act on customers' behalf. For firms it shapes supervisory expectations without new rules; for consumers it highlights both the potential to close advice gaps and the risks of opaque pricing and more convincing fraud.
